docs.text:
Cross-cutting ideas, trends, and frameworks in market research:

These environments afford opportunities for shallow skilling while restricting fuller development of capacities, with significant implications for AI's impact on human flourishing. capacity-conducive-environments 2026-07-03 2026-07-22 Environments that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing, providing alternatives to capacity-hostile conditions. These environments afford structured and unstructured embodied interactions necessary for intersubjective habituation of capacities. agential-control 2026-07-03 2026-07-25 The ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, a key component of being skilled that distinguishes skills from habits, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Skills require control over initiating the task, whereas habits are merely triggered by environmental cues. habituation-process 2026-07-03 2026-07-25 The gradual process of becoming skilled through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to demands of individual cases, with critical implications for AI's impact on skill development. Skill development cannot be learned through testimony alone but requires practice, encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure. intersubjectivity-in-skilling 2026-07-03 2026-07-22 The shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill. Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to instill not only mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill. embodiment-in-skilling 2026-07-03 2026-07-22 The essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities, particularly social and moral skills. Embodied interaction is critical for recognizing others as moral agents and forming meaningful relationships. ai-deskilling-structural-problem 2026-07-03 2026-07-22 The phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue. ai-adoption-selection-bias 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. ai-adoption-methodological-innovation 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 Methodological advances in measuring AI adoption, particularly the shift from occupational exposure scores to direct firm-level spending data. methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. pepm-metric 2026-07-15 2026-07-15 PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric measures the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level by calculating monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained adoption begins. ai-adoption-intensity-terciles 2026-07-15 2026-07-15 Methodology categorizing firms based on AI adoption intensity, dividing them into high (top tercile) and low (bottom two terciles) intensity groups based on PEPM metric. developmental-perfectionism 2026-07-15 2026-07-22 Neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life, providing the analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. narrow-field-of-affordances 2026-07-17 2026-07-22 An environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities, a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. epistemic-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-07-22 The human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis), which are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions. social-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-07-22 The human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life, including moral capacity and relational capacity. creative-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-07-22 The human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces, which enable innovation and adaptation. volitional-capacity 2026-07-18 2026-07-22 The human capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow in order to achieve intrinsically valuable goals, treated as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities. plan-following 2026-07-25 2026-07-25 Plan-following refers to the execution of pre-determined plans without exercising agential control over the planning process itself. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this represents a habitual mode of action where individuals respond to environmental triggers rather than initiating and adjusting plans through self-deliberation.

docs.title: Studies
docs.text:
Key research studies and reports:

Page First Observed Last Updated Description pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer 2026-06-25 2026-06-27 PwC's comprehensive analysis of over one billion job advertisements examining AI's impact on the global labor market. mrii-2026-market-research-study 2026-06-28 2026-06-28 The Market Research Institute International 2026 global study represents the fourth annual comprehensive analysis of market research and insights professionals worldwide. burning-glass-beyond-binary 2026-06-28 2026-06-28 Published in January 2026 by the Burning Glass Institute, "Beyond the Binary" represents a landmark analysis challenging the conventional wisdom that AI will either automate or augment jobs. ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study 2026-07-03 2026-07-15 A comprehensive analysis of how AI adoption affects employment patterns across 21,559 firms, using observed AI spending data linked to workforce records. Shows high-intensity adopters grow headcount by 10.2% and entry-level roles by 12.0%. ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem 2026-07-10 2026-07-25 Avigail Ferdman's 2026 paper in AI & Society presenting a structural analysis of how AI systems can undermine human capacities through systemic environmental conditions rather than individual failings. Introduces the critical distinction between capacity-hostile and capacity-conducive environments, analyzes the role of agential control and habituation in capacity development, and examines how Artificial Personal Assistants may create capacity-hostile environments by encouraging plan-following rather than plan-forming. The paper argues that deskilling should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions rather than merely an individual responsibility issue.

docs.text:
Expanded definition based on Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Agential control is the ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, which is a key component that distinguishes skills from habits.

According to Ferdman, skills require control over initiating the task, whereas mere habits do not: they are elicited in response to environmental triggers. An agent who performs out of habit, in response to triggers in the environment, is less skilled compared to the agent who initiated the activity and has full agential control over it.

This concept is critical for understanding the distinction between [[plan-forming]] (which requires agential control) and plan-following (which is more habitual). In market research contexts, maintaining agential control is essential for developing expertise in research design, data interpretation, and strategic decision-making.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: AI Adoption Intensity Terciles is a methodology developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to categorize firms based on the intensity of their AI adoption, measured by the PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. Firms are classified as AI adopters when they have three consecutive months of at least $100 in AI vendor spending
  2. Adoption intensity is measured as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over the first three months after adoption
  3. Among treated firms, PEPM values are sorted and divided into three equal groups (terciles):
  4. High intensity: top tercile (most intensive AI adopters)
  5. Medium intensity: middle tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom tercile (least intensive AI adopters)
  7. For analysis, firms are often grouped as:
  8. High intensity: top tercile
  9. Low intensity: bottom two terciles combined

docs.title: Rationale for Tercile Approach
docs.text:
• Allows researchers to examine differential impacts of AI adoption based on intensity
  • Reveals that not all AI adopters experience the same employment effects
  • Helps address selection bias by comparing firms with similar eventual adoption intensity
  • Shows that substantial employment gains are concentrated among high-intensity adopters

docs.title: Key Findings Using Intensity Terciles
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters grew total employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • High-intensity gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months, suggesting a learning curve
  • Employment gains were broad across roles for high-intensity adopters (engineering, sales, administration, customer service)

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: This methodology revealed a critical insight often missed in prior research: AI's labor market effects differ substantially based on adoption intensity. Studies that treat all adopters the same may miss these nuanced patterns.

docs.title: Ramp-Revelio Methodology
docs.text:
The study introduces the AI Spend Per Employee Methodology (PEPM):

  1. Adoption definition: Three consecutive months of ≥$100 AI vendor spend
  2. Intensity measure: PEPM = (sum of first 3 months' AI spend) / (3 × baseline headcount)
  3. Intensity stratification: Low (bottom two PEPM terciles), High (top PEPM tercile)
  4. Comparison design: Later adopters within same intensity group

This approach overcomes four critical limitations of prior methods:

  1. Direct observation: Measures actual adoption behavior rather than theoretical exposure
  2. Timing precision: Captures exact adoption month rather than imputed timing
  3. Intensity dimension: Reveals differential effects by adoption intensity
  4. Firm-level specificity: Avoids occupational aggregation that masks firm differences

docs.title: Observed Spending Threshold
docs.text: The $100/month threshold excludes one-off experiments while capturing sustained adoption, addressing the "Is this really AI adoption?" question that plagues survey-based approaches.

docs.title: PEPM Metric
docs.text: Using baseline headcount in the denominator makes intensity comparable across firm sizes and keeps employee scale predetermined relative to adoption timing.

docs.title: Staggered Treatment Design
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework accounts for heterogeneous treatment timing, avoiding biases in traditional event-study approaches.

docs.title: Evidence of Impact
docs.text: This methodological innovation revealed findings invisible to exposure-based studies: - Only high-intensity adopters (+10.2% headcount growth) showed significant employment effects - Entry-level roles grew 12.0% among high-intensity adopters, contradicting exposure-based predictions - Effects concentrated in Information sector (+13.4% growth), not uniformly distributed

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological shift has critical implications:

  • Vendor evaluation: Must measure actual usage intensity, not just adoption status
  • Impact assessment: Requires tracking spending patterns over time, not binary adoption
  • Benchmarking: Industry comparisons must account for intensity differences
  • ROI calculation: Benefits appear only above critical intensity thresholds

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This innovation directly addresses the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and explains the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies observed across research. It represents a critical advance over the pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index used in pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text:
For market research organizations, adopting this methodological innovation means: - Tracking actual AI spending rather than adoption claims - Measuring intensity through normalized spending metrics - Comparing against firms with similar pre-adoption characteristics - Focusing on sustained usage patterns rather than initial adoption

Without these methodological improvements, organizations risk misattributing effects or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns—precisely what the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study demonstrates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. As rigorously documented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, these selection effects mean AI adopters were already distinct from non-adopters before AI adoption, creating significant methodological challenges.

docs.title: Key Evidence
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study demonstrates dramatic pre-adoption differences:

Characteristic AI Adopters Never Adopters Difference Headcount (mean) 144.2 103.9 +40.3* Engineering share 26.8% 18.6% +8.2* Entry-level share 42.1% 50.4% -8.3* YoY growth (median) 6.0% 1.6% +4.4* Mean salary $110,346 $93,847 +$16,499* Tech-adjacent sector 54.2% 25.9% +28.3* VC-backed 34.0% 9.5% +24.5*

*Statistically significant at p<0.01

docs.title: Methodological Implications
docs.text:
This selection bias creates three critical challenges for AI impact research:

  1. Confounded comparisons: Simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons conflate AI effects with pre-existing differences
  2. Pre-trend divergence: Adopters were already on different growth trajectories before adoption (see Figure 4 in Ramp-Revelio study)
  3. Sector concentration: AI adoption heavily concentrated in Information (53.7%), Finance (43.6%), and Professional Services (36.0%)

docs.title: Addressing the Bias
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study employs sophisticated methods to address selection bias:

  • Preferred comparison: Later adopters within the same eventual intensity group
  • Sector fixed effects: Controlling for industry composition differences
  • Event-time analysis: Tracking pre-treatment parallel trends
  • Intensity stratification: Separating low vs. high adoption intensity effects

This approach revealed that only high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no significant change.

docs.title: Contrast with Exposure-Based Studies
docs.text: This selection bias explains why exposure-based studies (like pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer) often produce different findings than spending-based studies: - Exposure scores cannot distinguish firms that adopt AI from those that don't - They assume uniform adoption effects across firms with identical workforce composition - They miss the critical intensity dimension revealed by actual spending data

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This concept has profound implications for insights organizations:

  • Vendor selection: AI tools adopted by leading firms may reflect pre-existing advantages rather than causal benefits
  • Implementation strategy: Success depends on organizational readiness, not just tool adoption
  • Impact measurement: Must account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI initiatives
  • Benchmarking: Comparing against industry averages without controlling for selection effects is misleading

It explains why the employment gains documented in that study are concentrated among high-intensity adopters in specific sectors, rather than across all AI adopters.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, addressing selection bias requires: - Never comparing AI adopters to non-adopters without controlling for pre-existing differences - Measuring adoption intensity (PEPM) rather than binary adoption status - Using staggered adoption timing in evaluation designs - Focusing on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact

Without these precautions, organizations risk attributing pre-existing advantages to AI adoption or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns.

docs.title: Ai democratization
docs.text: AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI democratization describes how artificial intelligence makes advanced capabilities accessible by automating complex expert tasks, thereby reducing expertise requirements for certain occupations. As quantified in Figure 2 of the PwC 2026 report, this process affects 52% of global job postings. Concrete examples include [[recruiters]] (AI automates CV screening while humans handle contract negotiation) and [[inventory-clerks]] (AI manages stock optimization while humans perform physical movement). Figure 3 demonstrates democratization is particularly strong in high AI exposure jobs, where expertise requirements decrease significantly. Crucially, Figure 11 reveals that despite reduced expertise demands, democratized roles maintain high epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability, or interpersonal skills. The report warns that while democratization expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform data analysis), it may compress career ladders and reduce skill development opportunities without targeted interventions. This concept represents one of two primary pathways (alongside ai-professionalization) in AI's labor market restructuring. Organizations can leverage democratization through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Supply and Demand' dimension, redesigning roles to balance AI efficiency with human execution. The trend is accelerating post-2022, as shown in Figure 9's widening skill transformation gap, requiring proactive workforce planning to ensure equitable access to emerging opportunities in democratized roles.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The AI deskilling structural problem refers to the phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue.

docs.title: Key Insights from Ferdman
docs.text:
Ferdman's analysis provides several critical insights about this structural problem:

  1. Beyond Individual Responsibility: "Framing deskilling as a matter of individual responsibility—expecting people to simply will themselves to cultivate 'the arts of personhood'—overlooks crucial structural aspects of the problem."

  2. Environmental Dependence: "To a large extent, we develop and exercise our epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities in response to our social and material environment."

  3. Capacity Impoverishment: "A deficient environment can lead to deskilling of our core human capacities, and to the subsequent devaluation of their worth as they continue to weaken."

  4. Structural Solutions Needed: Rather than focusing only on how human agents ought to engage with AI tools, we should ask "what kind of socio-technical environments would be best for the cultivation of our personhood."

docs.title: Capacity vs. Skill Distinction
docs.text:
Ferdman makes an important distinction between general skill deskilling and capacity deskilling:

  • Skill Deskilling: May be innocuous (e.g., hunting, basket-weaving) as "skill obsolescence has always been part of human history, where technological developments free up time and resources for the cultivation of other skills."

  • Capacity Deskilling: Always problematic because "the deskilling of our core human capacities is bad because inadequate development of these capacities can lead to 'capacity impoverishment', which, in turn, diminishes us as humans and undermines our flourishing."

docs.title: Structural Mechanisms
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies several structural mechanisms through which AI creates deskilling environments:

  1. Narrow Affordance Fields: AI systems that "restrict, limit or create a narrow field of affordances for capacity development and exercise"

  2. Disembodied Interaction: Environments that reduce opportunities for embodied interaction necessary for social and moral capacity development

  3. Habituation Disruption: Systems that "deprive the user of the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature"

  4. Value Erosion: When environments fail to support "shared valuing" of capacities, leading to their devaluation and atrophy

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For the market research industry, the structural nature of AI deskilling has significant implications:

  • The entry-level-squeeze represents a structural challenge to traditional capacity development pathways
  • The human-operating-model-gap reflects the structural mismatch between AI capabilities and human capacity development needs
  • Research organizations must design capacity-conducive environments rather than expecting individuals to resist deskilling
  • Evaluation frameworks should measure capacity cultivation alongside productivity metrics

docs.title: Ai job future framework
docs.text: A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The AI Job Future Framework, introduced in Figure 6 of PwC's 2026 report, provides a structured methodology to assess AI's occupational impact through four critical questions: (1) Expertise: How is AI changing required human expertise? (e.g., democratization reduces expertise needs while professionalization increases them); (2) Supply and Demand: How might job demand and worker supply shift as AI reshapes roles?; (3) AI's limitations: Where is human oversight needed for quality control or atypical cases?; and (4) Environmental forces: How do regulations, business bottlenecks, or ethics constrain AI adoption? The report demonstrates the framework's application across diverse occupations: For [[pharmacists]], AI handles prescription processing (Expertise shift) but humans manage patient counseling (AI's limitations); for [[software-developers]], AI generates code but humans focus on architecture (Environmental forces). Figure 9 validates the framework by showing how high AI exposure roles undergo 2.2x faster skill changes, directly addressing the Supply and Demand dimension. Organizations using this tool can anticipate skill shifts, redesign roles, and develop targeted training—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' (Figure 12). The framework also explains wage dynamics: roles requiring human oversight of AI (Question 3) command higher premiums, as seen in Figure 15's 62% average AI skill premium. By systematically addressing these questions, employers can transform AI disruption into opportunity, while workers identify future-proof career paths in the evolving labor market. This methodology has become essential for strategic workforce planning in the AI era.

docs.title: New Evidence and Refinement

That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

The value-chain-shift concept further explains this dynamic - as AI makes answers faster and cheaper, the answers themselves become less differentiated, pushing value creation toward higher-order strategic functions.

docs.title: Relationship to Skills Development

A critical finding from the MRII study reveals a professionalization paradox: - Professionals prioritize learning technical AI skills - Leaders value business acumen, communication, and strategic influence more highly

This disconnect threatens to undermine the professionalization process, as organizations may automate tasks without adequately developing the human capabilities needed for the elevated roles.

docs.title: Update 2026-07-25
docs.text:
Expanded definition based on Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Capacity-conducive environments actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing. These environments afford structured and unstructured embodied interactions necessary for intersubjective habituation of capacities.

Key characteristics: - Provide opportunities for embodied interaction essential for social and moral skill development - Encourage agents to exercise agential control over initiating activities - Support intersubjective learning through mentorship and shared valuing of capacities - Create space for the gradual habituation process involving encountering and overcoming challenges - Balance automation with opportunities for plan-forming activities

In market research contexts, capacity-conducive environments include: - Team-based research design sessions that blend AI tools with human creativity - Client workshops that prioritize face-to-face interaction for complex problem-solving - Mentorship programs that guide junior researchers through the habituation process - Research processes that maintain appropriate challenges requiring human judgment

See embodiment-in-skilling, intersubjectivity-in-skilling, and agential-control for related concepts.

docs.title: Update 2026-07-25
docs.text:
Expanded definition based on Ferdman's structural analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Capacity-hostile environments restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for the development and exercise of core human capacities. These environments afford opportunities for shallow skilling while restricting fuller development of capacities, with significant implications for AI's impact on human flourishing.

Key characteristics: - Restrict opportunities for embodied interaction necessary for social and moral skill development - Create environments where users respond to triggers rather than exercising agential control - Undermine the intersubjective dimension of skill development by removing human mentors - Reduce opportunities for habituation through encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure - Encourage plan-following rather than plan-forming activities

In market research contexts, capacity-hostile environments may emerge when: - AI tools automate routine analytical tasks without preserving space for judgment development - Research processes become disembodied through excessive digital mediation - Researchers become overly reliant on AI for insight generation rather than developing their own interpretive skills

See narrow-field-of-affordances, ai-deskilling-structural-problem, and plan-following for related concepts.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Creative capacities are the human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces, which enable innovation and adaptation. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing and require specific conditions for their development and exercise.

docs.title: Core Characteristics
docs.text:
Ferdman's analysis identifies several fundamental aspects of creative capacities:

  • Novel Combination: Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Conceptual Transformation: Transforming a conceptual space without relying merely on luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures
  • Innovation Enabler: Essential for generating new solutions to complex problems
  • Adaptation Capacity: Critical for responding to novel situations and unexpected events

docs.title: Role in Life Planning
docs.text:
Ferdman specifically highlights the importance of creative capacities in life planning:

  • "Planning one's life also involves the capacity for creativity, insofar as planning is always incomplete, and executing the plan requires the ability to reconsider and respond to novel situations, surprises and unexpected events"

This demonstrates how creative capacities are not just for artistic pursuits but are fundamental to everyday human agency and adaptation.

docs.title: Development Process
docs.text:
Creative capacities develop through:

  • Habituation: A gradual process requiring practice, encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure
  • Intersubjective Learning: Requires mentorship to instill not only technical aspects but also the value of creativity
  • Embodied Interaction: Benefits from physical presence and sensory experience in creative environments
  • Agential Control: Requires the ability to initiate and adjust creative activities rather than merely following predetermined patterns

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies several ways AI systems can undermine creative capacities:

  • Automation of Routine Tasks: "Deprives the user of the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature"
  • Plan-Following Environments: Artificial Personal Assistants that encourage users to become "plan-followers rather than plan-formers"
  • Narrow Affordance Fields: Environments that restrict opportunities for novel combinations and conceptual transformations
  • Value Erosion: When environments fail to support shared valuing of creative capacities

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For the market research industry, creative capacities are particularly critical because:

  • Research innovation depends on creative capacity to develop novel methodologies
  • Insight generation requires making unfamiliar connections between data points
  • Client solutions often demand creative adaptation to unique business challenges
  • The entry-level-squeeze threatens traditional pathways for developing creative capacities through foundational work
  • The human-operating-model-gap reflects a mismatch between AI capabilities and creative capacity requirements

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Developmental Perfectionism is a neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life, providing the philosophical foundation for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this framework explains why the impoverishment of human capacities diminishes us as humans.

docs.title: Core Principles
docs.text:
Ferdman's analysis draws on Developmental Perfectionism to argue that:

  1. Flourishing as Unified Life: Human flourishing is "a complex, unified, and well-rounded life" (Hurka 1993) rather than the accumulation of isolated goods

  2. Intrinsic Value of Capacities: The competent exercise of human capacities is the manifestation of intrinsically valuable goods, making the capacities themselves intrinsically valuable

  3. Constitutive Relationship: Human capacities are constitutive of flourishing—"the value of being on the summit of Mt. Everest is gained from the competent exercise of a combination of capacities involved in climbing it, and not from simply being there"

  4. Developmental Process: Flourishing involves the development and exercise of capacities through a process of habituation rather than static achievement

docs.title: Human Capacities Framework
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism identifies four core categories of human capacities:

  1. Epistemic Capacities: Including theoretical rationality (thinking, considering reasons, forming beliefs) and practical rationality (phronesis or wisdom)

  2. Social Capacities: Including moral capacity and social/caring capacities for developing meaningful relationships

  3. Creative Capacities: Involving making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas and transforming conceptual spaces

  4. Volitional Capacity: The meta-capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow to achieve intrinsically valuable goals

docs.title: Implications for AI Deskilling
docs.text:
Ferdman uses Developmental Perfectionism to explain why AI-induced capacity deskilling is harmful:

  • Capacity Impoverishment: "Impoverished capacities (i.e., capacity-deskilling), therefore, lead to impoverished lives"
  • Structural Harm: Deskilling is not merely an individual failing but a structural problem that undermines the conditions for human flourishing
  • Beyond Instrumental Value: Human capacities have intrinsic value beyond their instrumental utility

docs.title: Contrast with Other Approaches
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism differs from:

  • Utilitarian Approaches: Which focus on maximizing outcomes rather than the development of capacities
  • Individual Responsibility Models: Which frame deskilling as a personal failing rather than a structural issue
  • Purely Instrumental Views of AI: Which evaluate AI solely on productivity metrics without considering capacity impacts

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For the market research industry, Developmental Perfectionism suggests:

  • Evaluation frameworks should measure capacity development alongside productivity
  • Research organizations should design environments that support the development of all four capacity types
  • The human-operating-model-gap reflects a mismatch between AI capabilities and human flourishing requirements
  • The value-chain-shift should be evaluated based on its impact on human capacity development

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Embodiment in skilling refers to the essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities, particularly social and moral skills. Embodied interaction is critical for recognizing others as moral agents and forming meaningful relationships, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
Ferdman's analysis draws on the Enactive Approach in cognition, which posits that:

  • "Embodied 'participatory sense-making' is constitutive of social cognition"
  • Social interaction itself and its emergent dynamics constitute an essential part of the cognitive process
  • "Meaning is generated and transformed in the interplay between the unfolding interaction process and the individuals engaged in it"

docs.title: Critical Role in Capacity Development
docs.text:
Embodiment plays several indispensable roles in human capacity development:

  1. Moral Recognition: "Without being embodied in a social interaction—without the return of the gaze of the other—we would be hard-pressed to recognize them spontaneously as moral agents"

  2. Shared Valuing: "The process of 'shared valuing' of the skill requires some degree of doing something with the mentor(s), creating a shared history and a participatory sense-making regarding both the product of the skill and the skill itself"

  3. Friendship Development: Disembodied interactions make it "harder to form meaningful friendship because technologically mediated virtue friendships require more discipline for a diminished experience"

  4. Capacity Triggering: Environments must not only afford but "encourage embodied interaction" to ensure "the activation of the capacities"

docs.title: Threats from Digital Environments
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies how disembodied digital environments undermine capacity development:

  • Reduced Moral Recognition: "Disembodied interaction requires the agent to exercise more mental efforts in attributing moral agency to the other"

  • Shallow Relationships: Without embodied interaction, it becomes "much more difficult to achieve" meaningful relationships compared to interactions with significant embodiment

  • Narrow Affordance Fields: Digital environments often provide "disconnected fields" of interaction that "fracture the user's affordance space" rather than offering opportunities for mutually informing and enriching capacities

  • Value Transmission Loss: The absence of embodied interaction limits opportunities for developing "shared valuing" of capacities

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For the market research industry, embodiment in skilling has critical implications:

  • Qualitative research methods depend on embodied interaction for deep understanding
  • Client relationship building requires physical presence for trust development
  • Team collaboration benefits from embodied interaction for shared understanding
  • The shift to remote work and AI tools creates risks for capacity deskilling through reduced embodied interaction

docs.title: Contrast with Disembodied Interaction
docs.text: Ferdman emphasizes that while shared valuing "might be achieved in the absence of any embodied interaction," it would be "much more difficult to achieve, compared to interactions that involve a significant level of embodiment."

docs.title: Entry level squeeze
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise.

docs.title: Capacity Development Challenges for Entry-Level Workers
docs.text: While recent evidence shows entry-level headcount is growing among high-intensity AI adopters, the nature of entry-level work is changing in ways that may affect capacity development for junior professionals.

docs.title: Deskilling Risks in Entry-Level Roles
docs.text:
The ai-deskilling-structural-problem framework reveals several risks for entry-level workers:

  • Reduced habituation opportunities: When AI automates routine tasks, entry-level workers lose "the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Shallow skill development: Entry into professions may become more superficial without proper mentoring
  • Disembodied learning: Digital workflows may limit embodied interaction necessary for social capacity development
  • Affordance shrinkage: Systematic reduction in action possibilities for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Structural Dimensions
docs.text:
These challenges are not merely individual responsibility issues but stem from structural conditions:

"We develop and exercise our epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities in response to our social and material environment" (Ferdman 2026). When entry-level environments become [[capacity-hostile]], junior professionals may struggle to develop the "arts of personhood" required for long-term success.

docs.title: Evidence from Research
docs.text: Studies show that young people growing up with digital tools already struggle with "everyday but essential" skills like empathy, time management, speaking to others, problem-solving and critical thinking (Halliday 2025). AI tools like artificial-personal-assistants could potentially exacerbate this deskilling.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these findings suggest:

  • Entry-level training programs must intentionally preserve opportunities for capacity development
  • Mentorship relationships are crucial for counteracting AI-mediated deskilling
  • Workflows should balance AI augmentation with human skill development
  • Organizations should design capacity-conducive environments for junior staff

The structural perspective emphasizes that "we cannot expect agents to be what Mitcham (2024) calls 'virtuous superheroes' and properly cultivate their human capacities if their social environment does not value the full maturation of these capacities."

See capacity-conducive-environments and habituation-process for related frameworks addressing these challenges.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Epistemic capacities are the human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis), which are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing rather than merely instrumentally valuable.

docs.title: Two Key Dimensions
docs.text: Ferdman's analysis identifies two fundamental aspects of epistemic capacities:

docs.title: Theoretical Rationality
docs.text:
• Thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating
  • Critical for knowledge acquisition and truth evaluation
  • Enables understanding of complex concepts and relationships
  • Requires engagement with evidence and logical reasoning

docs.title: Practical Rationality (Phronesis)
docs.text:
• Common sense or wisdom: doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason
  • Involves accurate understanding of one's situation and circumstances
  • Requires discernment: correct understanding of how the good and bad apply in particular contexts
  • Essential for critically reflecting on one's conceptions of a flourishing life

docs.title: Development Process
docs.text:
Epistemic capacities develop through:

  • Habituation: A gradual process requiring practice, encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure
  • Intersubjective Learning: Requires mentorship to instill not only mechanical aspects but also the value of epistemic capacities
  • Embodied Interaction: Benefits from physical presence and sensory experience in learning environments
  • Agential Control: Requires the ability to initiate and adjust epistemic activities rather than merely responding to environmental triggers

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies several ways AI systems can undermine epistemic capacities:

  • Critical Thinking Erosion: Evidence of "growing evidence of the erosion of critical thinking" as a result of over-reliance on AI
  • Decision-Making Impairment: Reduction in "decision-making and analytical reasoning" capabilities
  • Automation Bias: When users attribute "authority or excessive trust to an AI tool over advice from other sources"
  • Shallow Engagement: Environments that afford "opportunities for shallow skilling" rather than deep epistemic development

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For the market research industry, epistemic capacities are particularly critical because:

  • Research excellence depends on strong theoretical and practical rationality
  • Analytical reasoning is fundamental to transforming data into insights
  • Critical thinking is essential for evaluating research methodologies and findings
  • The entry-level-squeeze threatens traditional pathways for developing epistemic capacities
  • The human-operating-model-gap reflects a mismatch between AI capabilities and epistemic development needs

docs.text:
Expanded definition based on Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. The habituation process is the gradual development of skill through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to demands of individual cases, with critical implications for AI's impact on skill development.

Key aspects: - Skill development cannot be learned through testimony alone but requires practice - Involves encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure - Progresses through stages from novice to expert, with increasing sophistication - Requires embodied, intersubjective interaction with mentors and peers - Develops flexible links between thought and action that continue to evolve even after expertise is achieved

In market research contexts, the habituation process is threatened when AI tools: - Automate routine analytical tasks that previously provided opportunities for judgment development - Reduce opportunities for researchers to handle unexpected scenarios that build practical wisdom - Replace the gradual learning process with instant AI-generated insights

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Human capacities are core abilities that constitute human flourishing, including epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities, which are fundamental to being human and can be undermined by AI systems. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing rather than merely instrumentally valuable.

docs.title: Four Core Capacity Categories
docs.text: Ferdman's analysis, drawing on Developmental Perfectionism, identifies four fundamental categories of human capacities:

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
• Theoretical Rationality: Thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating
  • Practical Rationality (Phronesis): Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason, common sense or wisdom
  • Critical for knowledge acquisition, truth navigation, and informed decision-making

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text:
• Moral Capacity: Recognizing others as moral agents, making ethical judgments
  • Relational Capacity: Forming meaningful relationships of friendship and love
  • Essential for communal life, understanding others' perspectives, and moral development

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text:
• Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Transforming conceptual spaces without relying merely on luck or mechanical procedures
  • Enables innovation, adaptation, and novel problem-solving

docs.title: Volitional Capacity
docs.text:
• The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow
  • Required to achieve intrinsically valuable goals
  • Functions as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities

docs.title: Characteristics of Human Capacities
docs.text:
Ferdman emphasizes several key characteristics:

  1. Constitutive of Flourishing: These capacities are not merely instrumentally valuable but constitutive of human flourishing

  2. Developed Through Habituation: Capacities develop through a gradual process of habituation involving practice and error

  3. Intersubjective Development: Capacity development requires mentorship and shared valuing with others

  4. Embodied Nature: Full development requires embodied interaction and sensory experience

  5. Agential Control: Competent exercise requires control over initiating and adjusting activities

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies how AI systems can undermine human capacities:

  • Narrow Affordance Fields: Environments that restrict opportunities for capacity exercise
  • Disembodied Interaction: Reduced opportunities for embodied interaction necessary for social capacities
  • Habituation Disruption: Automation that deprives users of routine practice opportunities
  • Value Erosion: Environments that fail to support shared valuing of capacities

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For the market research industry, understanding human capacities is critical because:

  • Research excellence depends on all four capacity categories
  • The entry-level-squeeze threatens traditional pathways for capacity development
  • AI tools must be evaluated based on their impact on capacity cultivation
  • The human-operating-model-gap reflects a mismatch between AI capabilities and human capacity requirements

docs.title: Human operating model gap
docs.text: The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations.

docs.title: Workforce Composition Changes with AI Adoption
docs.text: Recent evidence reveals how AI adoption is reshaping workforce composition across roles, highlighting the growing gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower human system adaptation.

docs.title: Role-Specific Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study provides detailed evidence of how AI adoption affects different job functions:

  • Broad-based growth: High-intensity adopters showed growth across multiple roles:
  • Sales headcount: +10.3%
  • Administrative headcount: +7.8%
  • Engineering headcount: +7.3%
  • Customer service headcount: +6.3%

  • Scientist headcount: +5.6%

  • Entry-level expansion: Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% among high-intensity adopters

  • Managerial shifts: Manager-plus share fell by 1.52 percentage points despite overall growth

docs.title: Structural Workforce Shifts
docs.text:
These findings reveal several important patterns:

  1. Non-binary impact: AI adoption doesn't simply eliminate jobs but reshapes workforce composition
  2. Intensity matters: Only high-intensity adopters (top tercile of AI spend) showed significant growth
  3. Gradual emergence: Gains followed a learning curve, emerging 6-12 months after adoption
  4. Sector concentration: Effects were strongest in the Information sector

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these workforce shifts suggest:

  • AI is currently augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities in information work
  • Strategic AI investment may support growth across multiple functions
  • Entry-level positions may expand as firms scale with AI assistance
  • Workforce planning must account for the gradual nature of AI integration

The study notes that "the earliest signs of growth emerge roughly 6-12 months after adoption, perhaps after firms establish best practices, integrate AI tools into workflows, and are subsequently able to make new investments and hire staff."

docs.title: Bridging the Gap
docs.text:
To address the human operating model gap, market research firms should:

  • Develop AI adoption strategies that align with workforce development
  • Create pathways for employees to develop AI-augmented capabilities
  • Recognize that successful integration requires time for habituation
  • Design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for skill development

See value-chain-shift and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational structures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The intersubjectivity in skilling refers to the shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill. Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to instill not only mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Core Principles
docs.text:
Ferdman's analysis identifies several key aspects of intersubjective skilling:

  1. Mentorship Requirement: "Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to guide the novice into becoming an expert that engages in practice of the right kind"

  2. Shared Valuing: The mentor instills "not only the mechanical aspects of the skill, but, as importantly, the value of the skill, such that in the process of habituation, the skilled agent eventually comes to view the value of the skill as their own"

  3. Shared Intentions: In the mentor-mentee relationship, both parties develop "shared intentions" and come to have "shared valuing" of the skill

  4. Societal Dimension: Social practices performed by groups or whole societies can provide mentoring environments where "social practices are often what generates moral reasons for action"

docs.title: Importance for Capacity Development
docs.text:
Intersubjectivity plays several critical roles in human capacity development:

  • Value Transmission: Without learning the value of a capacity, individuals cannot develop motivation to cultivate it
  • Contextual Understanding: Mentors provide situated knowledge that cannot be conveyed through abstract principles alone
  • Error Correction: Mentors help novices recognize and learn from mistakes in ways that self-directed learning cannot
  • Identity Formation: As Ferdman notes regarding life-planning, "the identity of the person is, at least partly, constituted by their life plans"

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies how AI systems can undermine intersubjective skilling:

  • Artificial Personal Assistants: Reduce opportunities for human mentorship by providing AI-generated advice
  • Disembodied Interaction: Digital environments limit the depth of shared understanding possible through physical presence
  • Value Erosion: When capacities are not valued in the social environment, individuals "will not be inclined to become properly skilled, thereby entrenching a shallow level of the capacities"
  • Shared Valuing Loss: As Ferdman warns, when "enough persons do not value excellence or mastery of a human capacity (e.g., critical thinking), the capacity is in danger of atrophying"

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For the market research industry, preserving intersubjective skilling is crucial because:

  • Research expertise traditionally develops through mentorship and shared project experiences
  • Analytical reasoning skills require guidance from experienced practitioners
  • Client relationship skills depend on embodied interaction and shared understanding
  • The entry-level-squeeze threatens traditional mentorship pathways as AI automates foundational tasks

docs.title: Contrast with Individual Skill Development
docs.text: Unlike individual skill development models that focus solely on personal practice, the intersubjective approach recognizes that: - Skills develop within social contexts and practices - Value transmission is as important as technical instruction - Capacity development requires shared understanding of why the capacity matters

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. As demonstrated by the contrast between exposure-based studies and spending-based research like the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, methodological choices fundamentally shape conclusions about AI's labor market effects.

docs.title: Evidence of Heterogeneity
docs.text:
Study Type Primary Method Key Employment Finding Example Exposure-based Occupational AI exposure scores Negative impact on entry-level jobs Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) Spending-based Observed AI vendor payments Positive impact at high intensity Ramp-Revelio study Survey-based Executive adoption surveys Mixed or positive impacts Yotzov et al. (2026)

The Ramp-Revelio study documents this heterogeneity through direct comparison: - Exposure-based studies predict job losses in high-exposure occupations - Spending-based research shows job growth among high-intensity adopters - The discrepancy stems from methodological differences, not contradictory realities

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text: Three fundamental methodological differences drive these divergent findings:

docs.title: 1. Adoption Measurement
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Measure theoretical task feasibility ("could AI do this?")
  • Spending data: Measure actual adoption behavior ("is the firm paying for AI?")
  • Surveys: Capture self-reported usage ("do executives say they use AI?")

As the Ramp-Revelio study notes: "These estimates are closer to the Ramp–Revelio paid-adoption series than the firm-weighted BTOS benchmark, but they still measure a different object."

docs.title: 2. Intensity Dimension
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Typically binary or quintile-based
  • Spending data: Reveals continuous intensity effects (PEPM metric)
  • Surveys: Often lack precise intensity measures

The Ramp-Revelio study found only high-intensity adopters showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no change.

docs.title: 3. Selection Bias Handling
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Cannot distinguish adopters from non-adopters with identical workforce
  • Spending data: Enables direct comparison of adopters vs. later adopters
  • Surveys: Often lack pre-adoption data for comparison

The Ramp-Revelio study documents substantial pre-adoption differences that confound simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological heterogeneity creates critical challenges:

  • Conflicting guidance: Different studies recommend opposite actions based on methodology
  • Implementation uncertainty: Hard to predict AI impact without knowing intensity threshold
  • Evaluation complexity: Must select appropriate methodology for specific context
  • Vendor claims: AI providers may cite favorable methodology while ignoring others

docs.title: Strategic Response Framework
docs.text:
Market research organizations should adopt a methodologically sophisticated approach:

  1. Triangulate findings: Consider evidence from multiple methodological approaches
  2. Assess intensity: Focus on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact
  3. Control for selection: Account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI
  4. Contextualize results: Recognize sector-specific effects (e.g., concentrated in Information)

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept explains the contradictory findings between the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth) and exposure-based studies predicting job losses. It represents the methodological foundation for understanding the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and the value of the ai-adoption-methodological-innovation in spending-based measurement.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, navigating methodological heterogeneity requires: - Never relying on a single study's methodology for decision-making - Understanding the measurement approach behind any AI impact claim - Recognizing that "AI adoption" has no single empirical rate (as shown in Ramp-Revelio Figure 1) - Focusing on high-intensity implementation thresholds rather than binary adoption

Without this methodological sophistication, organizations risk making decisions based on incomplete or misleading evidence about AI's true impact.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A narrow field of affordances is an environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities, a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile-environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Core Characteristics
docs.text:
Ferdman's analysis identifies several key features of narrow fields of affordances:

  1. Limited Action Possibilities: Environments that "restrict, limit or create a narrow field of affordances for capacity development and exercise"

  2. Shallow Skilling Opportunities: These environments "afford opportunities for shallow skilling in the capacities, and restrict opportunities for a fuller, well-rounded development and exercise of capacities"

  3. Compensation Discouragement: Importantly, narrow fields not only restrict opportunities but also "discourage users from finding ways to compensate for the shrinkage"

  4. Systemic Nature: The problem becomes normatively problematic when the reduction in action possibilities is "systematic, enduring and deeply entrenched," constituting "affordance shrinkage"

docs.title: Examples in AI Context
docs.text:
Ferdman provides several concrete examples of narrow fields of affordances created by AI systems:

  1. Healthcare AI: Systems that "afford the possibility of offloading tasks to the machine" leading to "automation bias," which risks "the loss of the user's critical skills necessary for unexpected scenarios such as a system malfunction"

  2. Smartphone Interfaces: Providing "possibilities for interaction that are disconnected from other persons, such as swiping, clicking and scrolling" which "fractures the user's affordance space into disconnected fields, ultimately leading to alienation"

  3. Artificial Personal Assistants: Creating environments where users become "plan-followers rather than plan-formers" by offloading planning activities to AI systems

docs.title: Cumulative Impact
docs.text:
Ferdman emphasizes that the danger of narrow fields of affordances increases through cumulative effects:

  • Multiple Sphere Automation: "Automating multiple everyday human activities, across multiple spheres (e.g., writing, searching, planning, organizing, navigation, decision-making, entertainment, personal wellbeing)"
  • Compensation Difficulty: The cumulative effect makes it harder for users to find alternative avenues to compensate for capacity deskilling
  • Systemic Entrenchment: When narrow affordance fields become widespread, they create systemic conditions that are difficult for individuals to overcome

docs.title: Contrast with Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text: While narrow fields restrict capacity development, capacity-conducive-environments actively encourage it by: - Providing rich opportunities for embodied interaction - Encouraging rather than merely affording action possibilities - Supporting intersubjective habituation of capacities - Creating public goods infrastructure like community centers and public libraries

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For the market research industry, narrow fields of affordances could manifest as:

  • AI tools that automate foundational analytical tasks, creating an entry-level-squeeze
  • Research platforms that limit opportunities for creative problem-solving
  • Reporting systems that reduce opportunities for developing communication skills
  • Client interaction tools that narrow the field of relational possibilities

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) is a metric developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to measure the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level. It calculates monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained AI adoption begins.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
PEPM = (Σ²ₘ₌₀ AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ) / (3 × HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁)

Where: - AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ = AI vendor spend for firm i in month m after adoption - HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁ = baseline headcount in the month before adoption

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. AI adoption is defined as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  2. PEPM is calculated using AI spend over the first three months after adoption begins
  3. Baseline headcount is measured in the month before adoption
  4. Firms are sorted into intensity groups:
  5. High intensity: top PEPM tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom two PEPM terciles

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
• Provides a direct, observed measure of AI adoption intensity rather than relying on occupational exposure scores
  • Allows researchers to distinguish between firms that adopt AI lightly versus intensively
  • Correlates closely with adoption of more complex AI products and tools (coding agents, APIs) versus simpler chat subscriptions
  • Enables analysis of differential impacts based on adoption intensity

docs.title: Key Findings Using PEPM
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters (top tercile) grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Gains emerged gradually, suggesting a "learning curve" as firms integrated AI tools

docs.text:
Expanded definition based on Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Plan-following refers to the execution of pre-determined plans without exercising agential control over the planning process itself. As analyzed in the paper, this represents a habitual mode of action where individuals respond to environmental triggers rather than initiating and adjusting plans through self-deliberation.

In market research contexts, plan-following manifests when researchers: - Rely on AI tools to generate research approaches without developing their own strategic thinking - Follow pre-packaged analytical templates without adapting to unique research challenges - Execute research processes mechanically without exercising judgment in unexpected scenarios

Plan-following becomes problematic when it replaces plan-forming activities, as it: - Undermines the development of practical wisdom - Reduces opportunities for habituation through encountering research challenges - Creates capacity-hostile environments that restrict opportunities for skill development

See plan-forming-vs-plan-following, agential-control, and ai-deskilling-structural-problem for related concepts.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The critical distinction between actively creating plans through self-deliberation (requiring agential control) versus executing pre-determined plans (more habitual), with significant implications for AI's impact on capacity development as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Plan-Forming
docs.text:
• Definition: The active process of creating plans through self-deliberation, involving:
  • Settling function: Managing finite cognitive resources when facing choices

  • Coordination function: Forming and organizing different types of plans and intentions

  • Capacity requirements:

  • epistemic-capacities: Theoretical rationality for self-deliberation on values/goals
  • [[practical-wisdom]]: Understanding effective means to ends and accurate assessment of circumstances
  • volitional-capacity: Willpower to initiate planning activity

  • creative-capacities: Ability to respond to novel situations and unexpected events

  • Development process: Requires habituation through embodied, intersubjective interaction where:

    "Learning to value a capacity is part of the process of its habituation... learning to value the capacity is a result of an ongoing, gradual process of habituation, which they haven't gone through" (Ferdman 2026)

docs.title: Plan-Following
docs.text:
• Definition: Executing pre-determined plans without exercising agential control over the planning process itself. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this represents a habitual mode of action where individuals respond to environmental triggers rather than initiating and adjusting plans through self-deliberation.

  • AI manifestation: When users rely on artificial-personal-assistants for life planning:

    "A user might begin with asking the APA to help them form a plan for finding a soulmate, find a career... The APA will propose a plan and help the user refine it... In this sequence of events, the user is not initiating the two functions of planning: settling and coordinating, but merely responding to the APAs recommendations"

  • Capacity impact: Leads to diminished development of:

  • Practical wisdom ("merely being well motivated is not sufficient... equipped with valuable life experience")
  • Volitional capacity ("making plans involves taking responsibility if the plan fails... Yet if an APA makes a plan that ends up failing, the user could more readily shift the responsibility to the APA")
  • Social capacities (reduced shared experience with others)

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text: This distinction explains why AI adoption creates the entry-level-squeeze: - Traditional entry-level roles provided opportunities for plan-forming in research design, client interaction, and analysis - AI tools increasingly handle these tasks through plan-following interfaces - Junior researchers lose opportunities to develop [[practical-wisdom]] through habituation - Creates a structural barrier to professional development that cannot be solved by individual upskilling alone

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: Ferdman cites evidence that "young people growing up with the smartphone struggle with 'everyday but essential' skills like empathy, time management, speaking to other people, problem-solving and critical thinking" (Halliday 2025), suggesting that reduced opportunities for plan-forming in digital environments has measurable impacts on capacity development.

docs.title: Seniorised roles
docs.text: The phenomenon where entry-level roles increasingly demand skills traditionally required in senior positions due to AI adoption.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Seniorised roles describe the accelerating trend where entry-level positions now require skills traditionally associated with senior roles, driven by AI automation of foundational tasks. Figure 8 in the PwC 2026 report provides compelling evidence: in the US top AI exposure quartile, seniorised entry-level job postings are projected to grow 35% between 2019-2025, while non-seniorised roles decline by 10%. This occurs because AI tools handle routine onboarding tasks (e.g., data entry for [[inventory-clerks]] or basic analysis for [[recruiters]]), compressing career ladders and elevating entry requirements. Common senior skills now appearing in entry-level descriptions include strategic decision-making frameworks, cross-departmental collaboration, client advisory capabilities, and complex problem-solving—particularly in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Figure 7 contextualizes this within broader market trends, showing high AI exposure quartile entry-level postings have flatlined since 2022, suggesting seniorisation may be a prerequisite for growth in AI-impacted roles. The report warns this trend could exacerbate early-career inequality if not balanced with structured mentorship, as new graduates face higher barriers without prior exposure to advanced skills. However, organizations using the ai-job-future-framework can mitigate risks by designing onboarding that combines AI tools with human skill development. The phenomenon represents a key manifestation of AI's impact on career progression, with implications for education systems needing to prepare students for accelerated responsibility in the AI era.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Social capacities are the human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life, including moral capacity and relational capacity. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing and require specific conditions for their development and exercise.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text: Ferdman's analysis identifies several fundamental aspects of social capacities:

docs.title: Moral Capacity
docs.text:
• Recognizing others as moral agents
  • Making ethical judgments and decisions
  • Understanding moral reasons for action
  • Developing shared valuing of moral principles

docs.title: Relational Capacity
docs.text:
• Forming meaningful relationships of friendship and love
  • Understanding others' perspectives
  • Participating in communal life
  • Building trust and mutual understanding

docs.title: Development Requirements
docs.text:
Social capacities develop through specific conditions that Ferdman emphasizes:

  • Embodied Interaction: "Without being embodied in a social interaction—without the return of the gaze of the other—we would be hard-pressed to recognize them spontaneously as moral agents"
  • Intersubjective Learning: Requires mentorship and shared valuing where "the mentor instills not only mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill"
  • Shared History: "Creating a shared history and a participatory sense-making regarding both the product of the skill and the skill itself"
  • Public Goods: Environments that include "community centers, quality public spaces, public libraries" that encourage embodied interaction

docs.title: Threats from Digital Environments
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies several ways digital environments can undermine social capacities:

  • Disembodied Interaction: "Disembodied interaction requires the agent to exercise more mental efforts in attributing moral agency to the other"
  • Shallow Relationships: Technologically mediated interactions provide "a diminished experience" of relationships
  • Narrow Affordance Fields: Digital environments that "fracture the user's affordance space into disconnected fields, ultimately leading to alienation"
  • Value Erosion: When environments fail to support shared valuing of social capacities

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For the market research industry, social capacities are particularly critical because:

  • Client relationship building depends on strong social capacities
  • Qualitative research methods require deep interpersonal understanding
  • Team collaboration benefits from embodied interaction
  • The shift to remote work and AI tools creates risks for social capacity deskilling
  • The human-operating-model-gap reflects a mismatch between AI capabilities and social capacity requirements
