docs.title: Superstar effect
docs.text: The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies, referred to as 'superstars', achieve a significantly higher productivity growth rate.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The 'superstar effect' identifies a critical divergence among AI adopters: the top 20% of most AI-exposed firms achieve dramatically higher productivity gains than peers. This effect was documented by pwc using orbis company financial data. As revealed in Figure 12 of the PwC 2026 report, these 'superstar' companies attained 163% average productivity growth in 2025—5 times higher than the 33.5% growth rate of most AI-exposed companies as a whole. This advantage has widened steadily since 2022, with superstars accelerating their lead while other AI-exposed firms maintain moderate growth. Figure 13 shows this productivity advantage translates to headcount growth, with superstar firms expanding employment 52.2% by 2025 versus 35.7% for least exposed quartiles. Crucially, Figure 14 demonstrates these gains are shared with workers through higher wage growth (24.4% vs 16.6% in 2025). The report attributes superstar status to three factors: strategic AI integration beyond automation (leveraging the ai-job-future-framework), investment in complementary human skills, and organizational agility in addressing [[ai's limitations]]. This creates a 'winner-takes-most' dynamic where superstars capture disproportionate value—evident in Figure 16's AI specialist hiring surge within these firms. The effect has profound implications: companies failing to achieve superstar status risk falling behind in the AI transformation, while workers in superstar firms gain through both wages and career opportunities in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Policymakers must address resulting market concentration through targeted support for mid-tier AI adopters.

docs.title: Value chain shift
docs.text: The value chain shift refers to the fundamental repositioning of where value is created within market research and insights organizations as AI capabilities advance.

docs.title: Sectoral Variations in AI Impact
docs.text: Recent research reveals that AI's impact on the value chain is unevenly distributed across sectors, with significant implications for how value is created within market research organizations.

docs.title: Sectoral Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study found that employment gains from AI adoption are concentrated in the Information sector:

  • Information sector: 13.4% headcount growth among high-intensity AI adopters
  • Professional and technical services: Positive but non-significant growth
  • All other sectors: Near-zero or imprecise effects

This pattern reflects the current state of AI adoption, which is "uniquely concentrated in Information" where "the most commercially mature AI gains appear clearest in coding-agent and software-engineering workflows."

docs.title: Implications for Market Research Value Chain
docs.text:
For market research firms, this sectoral variation suggests:

  1. Front-end transformation: Research design and data collection may see earlier AI integration
  2. Back-end resilience: Interpretation and strategic recommendation may remain more human-intensive
  3. Specialization opportunities: Firms focusing on information-intensive research may adopt AI more rapidly
  4. Competitive differentiation: Early AI adopters in research may gain productivity advantages

The study notes that "it is still early in the AI adoption curve" and "AI use cases may diffuse more slowly outside software and media." This suggests market research firms should anticipate a gradual shift in where value is created, rather than an immediate transformation.

docs.title: Strategic Considerations
docs.text:
Market research organizations should consider:

  • Where their work aligns with sectors experiencing the strongest AI impacts
  • How to position themselves to benefit from productivity gains in information processing
  • When to invest in high-intensity AI adoption versus more limited applications
  • How to develop workforce strategies that align with sector-specific AI adoption patterns

See human-operating-model-gap and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational value chains.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Volitional capacity is the human capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow in order to achieve intrinsically valuable goals, treated as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this capacity is fundamental to human flourishing and particularly vulnerable to AI-mediated environments.

docs.title: Core Characteristics
docs.text:
Ferdman's analysis identifies several critical aspects of volitional capacity:

  • Effort Exertion: The ability to apply sustained effort toward challenging goals
  • Difficulty Overcoming: Capacity to navigate obstacles and setbacks
  • Perseverance: Continued commitment to goals despite challenges
  • Growth Orientation: The capacity to develop and improve through effort
  • Meta-Function: "Developing and exercising any of the human capacities is difficult, which therefore requires the competent exercise of the capacity to will"

docs.title: Role in Capacity Development
docs.text:
Volitional capacity plays several essential roles in human development:

  • Capacity Initiation: Required to initiate the development of other capacities
  • Habituation Support: Necessary for engaging in the "gradual process of habituation" that develops skills
  • Error Navigation: Critical for "encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure"
  • Value Commitment: Enables commitment to the value of capacities beyond immediate utility

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies several specific ways AI systems can undermine volitional capacity:

  • Effort Reduction: Environments that afford opportunities for users "not exercising their capacity to will"
  • Automation Bias: When technology "replaces human activity without encouraging users to seek alternative avenues to exercise their capacities"
  • Plan-Following Environments: Artificial Personal Assistants that encourage users to become "plan-followers rather than plan-formers"
  • Convenience Culture: APA systems that are "constantly available, designed to be helpful, always prompting the user to see if they could be of further assistance"

docs.title: Structural Dimension
docs.text:
Ferdman emphasizes that the threat to volitional capacity is structural rather than individual:

  • Rather than expecting individuals to be "virtuous superheroes" who resist deskilling
  • Capacity-conducive environments should "encourage the volitional capacity without expecting agents to be virtuous superheroes"
  • The structural approach recognizes that environments must be designed to support volitional development

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For the market research industry, volitional capacity is particularly critical because:

  • Research excellence requires sustained effort through complex projects
  • Methodological innovation demands perseverance through trial and error
  • Client consulting often involves navigating difficult business challenges
  • The entry-level-squeeze threatens traditional pathways for developing volitional capacity through foundational work
  • The human-operating-model-gap reflects a mismatch between AI capabilities and volitional development needs

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: AI & Society is an academic journal published by Springer focusing on the social, ethical, and philosophical implications of artificial intelligence and digital technologies, where ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem was published. The journal provides a venue for critical reflection on AI's societal impacts.

docs.title: Journal Scope
docs.text: AI & Society publishes research examining: - Ethical dimensions of AI development and deployment - Social implications of AI technologies - Philosophical analyses of AI's impact on human agency and flourishing - Policy considerations for responsible AI governance - Critical perspectives on AI's role in society

docs.title: Significance of Ferdman Publication
docs.text:
The publication of "AI deskilling is a structural problem" in AI & Society (2026) 41:3001-3013 represents a significant contribution to the field because:

  • It introduces the critical distinction between capacity-hostile-environments and capacity-conducive-environments
  • It provides a structural analysis of how AI systems can undermine human capacities through environmental conditions rather than individual failings
  • It develops a philosophical framework connecting AI impacts to human flourishing through the lens of Developmental Perfectionism
  • It offers concrete analysis of how artificial-personal-assistants can create capacity-hostile environments

docs.title: Methodological Approach
docs.text: The journal typically publishes work that employs: - Philosophical analysis of AI's societal impacts - Interdisciplinary approaches combining ethics, philosophy of technology, and social theory - Critical perspectives that challenge purely instrumental views of AI - Structural analyses that move beyond individual responsibility frameworks

docs.title: Relevance to Market Research

Expanded analysis based on Ferdman's research in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Artificial Personal Assistants (APAs) are AI systems based on Large Language Models designed to assist with personal organization, life planning, and decision-making, with critical implications for capacity development.

Examples include: - Scheduling tools like Sunsama that "display tasks synced from various software, alongside your calendar and unfinished tasks... [and] schedule tasks logically into your next available time slot" - Life-planning assistants that help users "organize my life" and "find purpose" - Social validation tools that provide "interpersonal guidance" and "self-regulation"

APAs can create capacity-hostile-environments when they: - Encourage users to become plan-followers rather than plan-formers - Reduce opportunities for embodied, intersubjective habituation of capacities - Undermine the development of practical wisdom through real-world experience - Create narrow fields of affordances that restrict opportunities for capacity development

In market research contexts, APA-like tools may threaten epistemic, social, creative, and volitional skills when researchers become overly reliant on AI for research design, insight generation, and client communication.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework is an econometric approach for analyzing treatment effects when units receive treatment at different times, as implemented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to analyze the impact of AI adoption on employment.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Developed by Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) to address limitations of conventional two-way fixed effects event studies
  • Designed for staggered adoption designs where firms begin treatment (AI adoption) at different points in time
  • Estimates group-time average treatment effects separately for different adoption cohorts
  • Compares earlier adopters to later adopters in the same intensity group while the later adopters have not yet adopted

docs.title: Implementation in Ramp-Revelio Study
docs.text:
• Used to estimate the relationship between firm-level AI adoption and employment
  • Applied separately to low and high AI intensity adoption groups
  • For high-intensity adopters, compared firms that adopted early to firms that would eventually be high-intensity adopters but hadn't yet adopted
  • Included NAICS sector fixed effects to address selection into early AI adoption

docs.title: Advantages Over Traditional Methods
docs.text:
• Better suited to heterogeneous treatment timing than single two-way fixed effects event studies
  • Reduces bias that can occur when treatment effects are heterogeneous across adoption cohorts
  • Allows for more precise estimation of dynamic treatment effects
  • Provides cleaner pre-treatment diagnostics for parallel trends assumption

docs.title: Key Findings Enabled by This Framework
docs.text:
• Revealed that high-intensity AI adopters grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Showed that these gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months
  • Demonstrated that low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Provided evidence against predictions that AI adoption would lead to broad job losses

docs.title: Lightcast
docs.text: Lightcast (formerly Emsi Burning Glass) is a labor market analytics company that provides detailed data on job postings, skills demand, and workforce trends. The company aggregates and analyzes millions of job postings from across the internet to create comprehensive labor market intelligence.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Lightcast data serves as a primary source for PwC's Global AI Jobs Barometer analysis. According to the 2026 report, the analysis examined over one billion online job advertisements across six continents, with Lightcast providing the underlying job posting data.

docs.title: Data Collection Methodology
docs.text:
Lightcast gathers job posting data through:

  • Web scraping of major job boards and company career sites
  • Partnerships with job posting aggregators
  • Direct feeds from some large employers
  • Historical archives dating back to 2012 for certain markets

The company processes this raw data to extract structured information about required skills, qualifications, compensation, and other job characteristics.

docs.title: Application in PwC's Research
docs.text:
In the PwC 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, Lightcast data was used to:

  • Track changes in job posting volumes across different AI exposure levels
  • Analyze skill requirements and how they evolve over time
  • Calculate wage premiums for AI-related skills
  • Identify trends in entry-level hiring patterns
  • Measure growth in AI specialist positions

docs.title: Key Insights Enabled by Lightcast Data
docs.text:
Analysis of Lightcast data revealed several critical patterns:

  • AI specialist job postings grew eight times faster than total job postings from 2012-2025
  • Entry-level job postings in the highest AI exposure quartile flatlined after 2022
  • Skills needed for the most AI-exposed jobs are changing 2.2x faster than for the least exposed jobs
  • Wage premiums for AI skills reached 62% across all sectors in 2025

docs.title: Limitations and Considerations
docs.text:
While valuable, Lightcast data has certain limitations:

  • Primarily captures formal, online job postings (may miss informal hiring)
  • Coverage varies by country and time period
  • Skill extraction relies on natural language processing of job descriptions
  • May not fully capture internal mobility or promotions

Researchers using Lightcast data, like PwC, typically note these limitations and adjust their methodologies accordingly.

See also: pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer, pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index

docs.title: ORBIS
docs.text: ORBIS is a comprehensive global business information database maintained by Bureau van Dijk (a Moody's Analytics company). It provides detailed financial, ownership, and operational data on millions of companies worldwide, serving as a critical resource for business intelligence and economic research.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: In PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, ORBIS data served as the primary source for company-level analysis, particularly regarding productivity, headcount, and wage growth metrics across different levels of AI exposure.

docs.title: Data Coverage
docs.text:
ORBIS includes information on:

  • Over 400 million companies globally
  • Financial statements and performance metrics
  • Ownership structures and corporate hierarchies
  • Industry classifications using standard systems like NAICS
  • Employment data and executive information

For the PwC analysis, the database provided longitudinal data from 2018-2025 for companies with consistent reporting.

docs.title: Application in PwC's Research
docs.text:
PwC used ORBIS data to:

  • Measure productivity growth (revenue per employee) across AI exposure levels
  • Track headcount changes at companies in different AI exposure quartiles
  • Analyze wage growth patterns relative to AI adoption
  • Identify the "superstar effect" among highly AI-exposed companies

docs.title: Key Insights Enabled by ORBIS Data
docs.text:
Analysis of ORBIS data revealed several critical patterns:

  • The most AI-exposed companies showed 33.5% productivity growth (2018-2025) compared to 18.7% for least exposed
  • Headcount growth at most AI-exposed companies reached 52.2% versus 23.3% for least exposed
  • Wage growth at most AI-exposed companies reached 24.4% versus 5.6% for least exposed
  • The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies ("superstars") achieved 163% productivity growth

docs.title: Methodological Considerations
docs.text:
PwC's analysis using ORBIS data included several important methodological notes:

  • Focus on larger formal firms with annual turnover of at least $50m USD
  • Exclusion of companies that exited the market during the period (creating survivorship bias)
  • Potential bias toward larger, more formalized companies in some countries
  • Company AI exposure determined by NAICS sector classification

These considerations mean the analysis reflects patterns among established businesses rather than the entire economy, but still provides valuable insights into how AI adoption correlates with business performance.

See also: pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer, superstar-effect

docs.title: PwC
docs.text: PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) is a multinational professional services network and one of the Big Four accounting firms. It provides audit and assurance, tax, and advisory services to corporations, governments, and non-profit organizations globally. With operations in 157 countries and over 360,000 employees, PwC serves as a leading authority on economic and labor market trends.

docs.title: Relevance to AI and Market Research
docs.text: PwC has emerged as a pivotal publisher of research on artificial intelligence's impact on the global labor market. Its annual Global AI Jobs Barometer report analyzes trends using data from over one billion job advertisements, providing critical insights for the market research industry. The firm's proprietary pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index methodology has become a standard for measuring AI's workforce impact.

docs.title: Key Contributions
docs.text:
• Developed the epoch-score framework for measuring human capability reliance in occupations
  • Identified the dual trends of ai-democratization (52% of jobs) and ai-professionalization (22% of jobs)
  • Documented the superstar-effect where top AI-adopting companies achieve disproportionate productivity gains
  • Quantified wage premiums for ai-skills across economic sectors

PwC's research directly informs talent strategy for market research firms navigating AI adoption. Their data provides empirical validation for skills gap analyses and workforce planning.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Ramp is a financial operations platform that processes corporate card and bill pay transactions. It provides the AI Index for measuring AI adoption intensity through corporate spending data.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Ramp's data was central to the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, which linked Ramp's line-item spending data with Revelio Labs' workforce records to study AI's impact on employment.

docs.title: AI Index Methodology
docs.text:
• Identifies AI spend from line items using vendor and line-item classification
  • Captures spending on foundational large language models, GPU cloud, model serving and inference, coding agents, API tokens, AI image and video generators, and AI search and research software
  • Defines AI adoption as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  • Measures adoption intensity as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over first three months after adoption

docs.title: Data Collection
docs.text:
• Observes cleared spend at the line-item level, including date, amount, merchant, firm identifiers, and line-item detail
  • Aggregates records to the firm-month level
  • Requires firms to have at least six consecutive months of total Ramp spend of $5,000+ to qualify for analysis

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: Ramp's data provides a direct measure of AI adoption through actual spending, overcoming limitations of occupational exposure scores and surveys. This revealed-adoption measure captures firms making sustained, organization-level AI purchases rather than one-off employee experiments.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Revelio Labs is a workforce intelligence platform that aggregates data from online professional profiles to construct longitudinal employment histories. It provides seniority classification and workforce composition data.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Revelio Labs' workforce data was central to the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, which linked Revelio's employment records with Ramp's AI spending data to study AI's impact on employment.

docs.title: Data Collection Methodology
docs.text:
• Aggregates information from millions of publicly available online professional profiles
  • Constructs longitudinal employment histories for individual workers
  • Each profile contains information on employers, job titles, employment dates, locations, and other career characteristics
  • Uses a seven-point seniority field to define:
  • Entry-level headcount: seniority 1-2
  • Non-entry headcount: seniority 3-7
  • Manager-plus headcount: seniority 4-7
  • Applies weighting methodology to adjust for differential platform usage and improve representativeness

docs.title: Data Validation
docs.text:
• Prior validation exercises show weighted Revelio measures closely track benchmark labor market statistics
  • Similar worker-level employment histories have been used extensively in academic research

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: Revelio Labs provides granular workforce data that enables analysis of not just total firm employment but also hiring, attrition, occupational composition, worker seniority, and other workforce characteristics difficult to observe in traditional data sources.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This chart compares AI adoption rates across different measurement methodologies. The Ramp/Revelio series tracks paid-AI adoption in their analytical panel, showing adoption rates rising from approximately 10% in early 2023 to over 60% by mid-2026. This is contrasted with U.S. Census estimates (17-20%), Atlanta Fed Survey of Business Uncertainty (78%), and Yotzov et al. executive survey estimates (69%). The visualization demonstrates that "AI adoption" lacks a single empirical rate due to varying measurement approaches - some capture broad organizational use while others measure only paid, sustained adoption with payment traces.

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
• Different methodologies yield dramatically different adoption rates (from 17% to 78%)
  • Ramp/Revelio measures sustained paid adoption requiring $100/month for 3 consecutive months
  • Executive surveys capture broader organizational awareness but may overstate actual implementation
  • The measurement approach fundamentally shapes conclusions about AI's economic impact

The pattern aligns with a task-based interpretation of early AI demand - sectors with workforces concentrated in software, analytical, and information-processing work show higher adoption rates.

  • Professional services adoption (36.0%) exceeds Manufacturing (22.8%)

docs.title: Figure 3: AI Adoption by Size and Engineering Share
Description
docs.text: This dual-chart visualization shows AI adoption patterns by firm characteristics. The left chart demonstrates adoption increases with firm size, rising from 12% among firms below 10 workers to 41-43% among firms above 250 workers. The right chart shows adoption peaks at 38.5% among firms with 15-30% engineering share, declining slightly at higher engineering concentrations. This suggests AI adoption is most common among firms with mixed workforces - sufficient technical capacity to evaluate AI tools but enough non-engineering work to drive cross-functional experimentation.

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
• Small firms (<10 workers) adopt AI at half the rate of large firms (>250 workers)
  • Adoption peaks at 38.5% for firms with 15-30% engineering share
  • Firms with no engineering presence still adopt AI at 9% rate
  • Optimal adoption occurs in organizations with balanced technical/non-technical composition

docs.title: Figure 4: Indexed Headcount and Pre-Trends: AI Adopters vs. Never Adopters
Description
docs.text: This event study chart compares indexed total headcount for AI adopters versus calendar-matched never-adopters. The series are already separated before adoption (-12 to 0 months), with adopters on a faster growth trajectory while never-adopters remain comparatively flat. This pre-existing divergence demonstrates why using never-adopters as the counterfactual would confound AI adoption effects with pre-existing firm growth differences.

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
• AI adopters showed 5-7% higher headcount growth than never-adopters even before adoption
  • The growth gap widens after adoption, reaching 15% by 24 months post-adoption
  • Pre-treatment divergence invalidates simple adopter vs. never-adopter comparisons
  • Selection bias is substantial in AI adoption studies using standard DiD approaches

docs.title: Figure 5: Indexed Headcount and Pre-Trends: AI Adopters vs. Not-Yet Adopters
Description
docs.text: This event study chart compares indexed total headcount for AI adopters versus later adopters (not-yet adopters) in the same eventual intensity group. Unlike Figure 4, the pre-treatment paths track closely, with both series aligned at 100 in event month -1. This alignment supports the parallel-trends assumption needed for valid causal inference, demonstrating that comparing earlier and later adopters within intensity groups provides a more appropriate counterfactual than using never-adopters.

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
• Pre-treatment headcount paths are nearly identical for adopters and not-yet adopters
  • Divergence begins approximately 6 months after adoption
  • Growth differential reaches 10% by 18 months post-adoption
  • Validates the Callaway-Sant'Anna methodology for staggered adoption designs

docs.text: This event study chart shows the employment impact of high-intensity AI adoption over time. High-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) experience gradually increasing headcount growth, with effects becoming statistically significant around 6 months post-adoption. By month 18, headcount is 32% higher (0.277 log points) compared to later adopters in the same intensity group, reaching 57% higher (0.452 log points) by month 24, though with wider confidence intervals in later periods.

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
• High-intensity AI adoption drives 10.2% total headcount growth over 24 months
  • Effects follow a learning curve, emerging gradually after adoption
  • Significant growth begins at 6-12 months as firms establish best practices
  • Low-intensity adopters show no statistically significant headcount changes

docs.text: This event study chart reveals that high-intensity AI adoption increases entry-level headcount by 12.0% over 24 months. The effect becomes statistically significant around 6 months post-adoption and continues growing throughout the observation window. This finding directly contradicts predictions that AI adoption would reduce junior employment opportunities, showing instead that intensive AI users expand their entry-level workforce.

docs.title: AI Spend Per Employee Methodology
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-03

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A direct measurement approach for quantifying firm-level AI adoption intensity by calculating monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after adoption begins. Developed by Ramp economists for the 2026 AI Jobs Impact Study, this methodology addresses limitations of occupational exposure scores and survey-based adoption measures.

docs.title: Calculation
docs.text:
PEPM_i = (Σ from m=0 to 2 of AI_{i,G_i+m}) / (3 × HC_{i,G_i-1})

Where: - AI_{it} = monthly AI vendor spend - G_i = first month of sustained AI adoption - HC_{i,G_i-1} = baseline headcount in month before adoption

docs.title: Implementation Steps
docs.text:
1. Adoption Definition: First month of earliest three-consecutive-month spell with ≥$100 AI spend monthly
  2. Intensity Measurement: Calculate PEPM using first three post-adoption months
  3. Group Classification: Low intensity = bottom two PEPM terciles, High intensity = top tercile
  4. Comparison Design: Compare earlier adopters to later adopters in same intensity group

docs.title: Advantages Over Alternative Methods
docs.text: Method Limitations PEPM Advantages Occupational exposure scores Vary only across occupations, not firms Measures actual firm adoption decisions Executive surveys Capture awareness not implementation Tracks payment data showing actual usage AI-related job postings Proxy for interest not adoption Measures direct financial commitment Resume AI skills Lagging indicator of adoption Captures immediate spending behavior

docs.title: Key Insights from Application
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters (PEPM top tercile) grew headcount by 10.2% over 24 months
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant employment changes
  • Adoption intensity correlates with use of complex AI tools (coding agents, APIs)
  • First three months of spending strongly predicts long-term adoption patterns

docs.title: Sectoral Variation
docs.text: PEPM reveals significant sector differences in adoption intensity: - Information sector firms show highest intensity adoption - Professional services demonstrate moderate intensity - Traditional sectors show minimal intensity despite some adoption

docs.text: This methodology provides market researchers with: 1. A concrete way to measure client AI adoption beyond self-reported surveys 2. Evidence that AI investment intensity predicts organizational growth 3. Framework for segmenting clients by true AI integration maturity 4. Validation that direct spending data outperforms proxy measures

docs.title: Epoch score
docs.text: The EPOCH score measures the reliance on human capabilities in various occupations.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The EPOCH score, pwc's proprietary metric, quantifies occupational reliance on human capabilities difficult for AI to replicate. Ranging 0-1, it evaluates dimensions including empathy, creativity, physical dexterity, and face-to-face interaction through job description analysis and expert assessment. Figure 10 of the 2026 report provides definitive validation: new tasks added to AI-exposed roles since 2022 show EPOCH scores 2.5 times higher in the top exposure quartile (0.47) versus bottom quartile (0.19), proving AI shifts work toward human-intensive activities. Figure 11 further demonstrates its significance by showing democratised roles (0.48) and professionalised roles (0.45) maintain substantially higher scores than low exposure roles (0.26), indicating both AI impact pathways increase human reliance. The methodology explains key economic trends: occupations with higher EPOCH scores in AI-exposed roles command greater wage premiums (Figure 15), as human skills become scarcer value drivers. Crucially, the score helps operationalize the ai-job-future-framework's 'AI's limitations' dimension by identifying tasks requiring human oversight. The report shows EPOCH scores are rising fastest in high-exposure roles (Figure 9), with the top quartile's score increasing 116% from 2023-2025. This metric has become essential for organizations mapping future skill requirements, particularly in designing professionalised-jobs and addressing the human elements of 'superstar' company success (Figure 12). Policymakers also use it to target workforce development initiatives where human capabilities provide sustainable competitive advantages.

docs.title: Pwc ai occupational exposure index
docs.text: PwC's proprietary methodology to measure the degree to which different occupations are exposed to AI capabilities.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: PwC's AI Occupational Exposure Index quantifies occupational susceptibility to AI through a multi-dimensional methodology. Ranging 0-1, it analyzes 2,000+ work activities across 800+ occupations, assessing technical feasibility, economic viability, and adoption timelines for AI automation. The 2026 report reveals 74% of jobs have meaningful exposure (quartiles 2-4), with the top quartile experiencing transformative impacts. Figure 3 demonstrates how the index interacts with expertise requirements, showing high-exposure jobs either increase (professionalisation) or decrease (democratization) expertise demands. The methodology underpins critical findings: Figure 7 uses it to segment entry-level job trends, Figure 9 to analyze skill change velocity (top quartile changing 2.2x faster), and Figure 12 to correlate exposure with productivity. Notably, the index evolved to incorporate generative AI capabilities post-2022, explaining accelerated impacts observed after ChatGPT's release. Organizations apply it to identify at-risk roles, prioritize reskilling, and benchmark against industry peers—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' where top-quartile firms achieve 163% productivity growth. The report details sector-specific adaptations (e.g., healthcare's focus on diagnostic support roles), making it versatile for workforce planning. When combined with the epoch-score, the index forms the empirical foundation of the ai-job-future-framework, enabling organizations to systematically address all four framework questions. Its longitudinal design (2012-2025 data) provides unprecedented insight into AI's accelerating labor market transformation.

docs.title: Ai specialist roles
docs.text: Job roles specifically focused on the development, implementation, and maintenance of AI systems, growing eight times faster than total job postings.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI specialist roles are experiencing explosive growth, expanding eight times faster than total job postings according to Figure 16 of the PwC 2026 report. From a 2012 baseline of zero, these roles reached 11.0x growth by 2025 versus 2.0x for total postings, with acceleration intensifying post-2022. Figure 16b shows pervasive sector adoption: Technology, Media and Telecoms leads at 11.4% of sector roles, followed by Health Industries (4.0%), Financial Services (3.0%), and Manufacturing (2.0%). Core responsibilities include AI system architecture, prompt engineering, ethical governance, and domain-specific integration—often blending technical and business skills. Figure 15 confirms these roles command significant wage premiums averaging 62%, with Consumer Markets reaching 118%. The report identifies three growth drivers: urgent demand for AI implementation expertise, the need to address [[ai's limitations]] in quality control and edge cases, and regulatory compliance requirements. Crucially, Figure 12 links this growth to the 'superstar effect', as top-performing AI-exposed companies achieve 163% productivity growth by strategically deploying these specialists. Unlike traditional tech roles, modern AI specialists increasingly operate in hybrid functions (e.g., AI-augmented [[pharmacists]] or [[financial-analysts]]), requiring both domain knowledge and technical proficiency. This trend positions AI specialization as a critical career pathway across the economy, with implications for education systems needing to develop curricula aligned with the ai-job-future-framework.

docs.title: Democratised jobs
docs.text: Democratised jobs are occupations reshaped by AI to demand less human expertise, representing 52% of advertised positions globally.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Democratised jobs—where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans—constitute 52% of global postings but show distinct market patterns. Figure 2 illustrates this through roles like [[inventory-clerks]] (AI automates inventory management but humans move stock) and [[recruiters]] (AI screens CVs but humans negotiate contracts). While numerous, Figure 4 shows they've added skills at half the pace of professionalised roles (33% vs 68% growth 2018-2025), and Figure 5 confirms slower salary growth (26% vs 37% since 2021). However, Figure 11 reveals a critical nuance: democratised roles maintain the highest average epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability in unstructured environments, or interpersonal interactions. This explains why these roles remain resilient despite reduced expertise requirements. The report warns that while democratisation expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform complex analysis via AI tools), it may compress career ladders without structured progression paths. Figure 9 contextualizes this within skills transformation, showing democratised roles still experience 2.2x faster skill changes than low-exposure jobs. Organizations can leverage this trend through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Environmental forces' dimension, designing roles that combine AI efficiency with uniquely human execution—particularly valuable in sectors like retail and logistics where physical interaction remains essential.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Entry-level job postings in quartiles with lower AI exposure continue to grow, while those in the highest AI exposure quartile have flatlined since 2022. As documented in multiple studies, these positions represent critical training grounds for developing professional expertise through the habituation process.

docs.title: Contradictory Evidence
docs.text:
Recent research presents seemingly contradictory findings about entry-level job trends:

  • Exposure-based studies: Predict decline in entry-level roles due to AI automation
  • Spending-based research: Shows growth in entry-level roles among high-intensity AI adopters

The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study resolves this contradiction by revealing: - High-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) grew entry-level headcount by 12.0% - Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change - Gains emerged gradually, reaching significance around 6-12 months post-adoption - Growth was broad across functions: engineering, sales, admin, customer service

This explains why the entry-level-squeeze concept remains relevant despite overall growth—entry-level roles are growing only among firms making substantial AI investments.

docs.title: Structural Tensions
docs.text:
Entry-level positions face three competing forces:

  1. Automation pressure: AI systems can perform foundational tasks that traditionally served as training grounds
  2. Capacity development need: Junior staff require opportunities to develop through the habituation process
  3. Strategic value: High-intensity AI adopters recognize entry-level roles as essential for scaling AI-enhanced operations

This creates a bifurcated market where entry-level opportunities are shrinking in low-AI firms but expanding in high-AI firms.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
The industry faces a critical challenge:

  • Traditional pathways: Junior researchers developing through manual analysis are becoming rare
  • New requirements: Entry-level roles increasingly demand human-intensive-skills alongside AI literacy
  • Capacity risk: Over-automation threatens the embodiment-in-skilling and intersubjectivity-in-skilling needed for deep expertise

The ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem study warns that without careful design, AI tools may create capacity-hostile environments where junior researchers miss critical development opportunities.

docs.title: Strategic Framework for Organizations
docs.text: Market research firms should adopt a dual approach:

docs.title: For High-Intensity AI Adopters
docs.text:
• Preserve foundational tasks: Create 'capacity zones' where junior staff develop without AI assistance
  • Structured progression: Gradually increase AI tool complexity as researchers develop
  • Mentorship integration: Pair AI tools with human guidance to maintain intersubjectivity-in-skilling

docs.title: For All Organizations
docs.text:
• Measure capacity development: Track skill progression alongside productivity metrics
  • Design capacity-conducive workflows: Ensure AI tools extend rather than replace the learning journey
  • Value human-intensive-skills: Recognize that AI augmentation increases demand for uniquely human capacities

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This analysis synthesizes findings from the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth at high-intensity adopters) and ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem (warning about capacity erosion risks). It explains how the entry-level-squeeze operates within a context of overall growth among high-AI firms, creating a bifurcated job market.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals managing entry-level talent: - Never automate foundational analytical tasks that provide essential habituation - Create clear pathways showing how junior staff progress from manual to AI-enhanced work - Balance AI efficiency with capacity development opportunities - Measure both productivity gains and capacity development outcomes

Without this balanced approach, organizations risk creating researchers who lack the deep intuition needed to navigate complex, novel challenges—precisely where AI systems reach their limits.

docs.title: Professionalised jobs
docs.text: Professionalised jobs are occupations reshaped by AI to demand more human expertise, representing 22% of advertised positions globally.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Professionalised jobs—where AI automates less expert tasks, leaving more expert tasks for humans—show robust positive dynamics per the PwC 2026 report. Figure 4 demonstrates these roles have demanded additional skills at twice the rate of democratised roles (68% vs 33% growth 2018-2025), with the gap widening significantly since 2022. Figure 5 confirms they've achieved 42% faster salary growth (37% vs 26% since 2021) and twice the job posting growth (39% vs 17% from 2018-2025). Figure 11 reveals their high average epoch-score of 0.45, indicating substantial reliance on human capabilities despite elevated expertise requirements. The report identifies exemplar roles like [[environmental-engineers]] (where AI handles data collection but humans focus on complex modeling) and [[pharmacists]] (where AI manages prescriptions but humans provide patient counseling). These occupations thrive because AI handles routine analysis, freeing humans for strategic judgment and innovation—validating the 'Expertise' dimension of the ai-job-future-framework. Figure 13 shows professionalised-job employers also achieve 52.2% headcount growth by 2025 (versus 35.7% for least exposed firms), suggesting these roles drive organizational expansion. The data positions professionalisation as a high-value career pathway, though it requires continuous upskilling. Workers in these roles increasingly need to address [[ai's limitations]] through quality oversight and atypical case management, creating sustainable competitive advantages in the AI economy.

docs.title: Ai skills
docs.text: Technical and domain-specific skills related to artificial intelligence, with wage premiums averaging 62% across sectors.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Wage premiums for AI skills have risen to 62% (from 57% in 2025), with significant sectoral variation documented in Figure 15 of the PwC report. Consumer Markets leads at 118%, followed by Technology, Media and Telecoms (84%), Energy, Utilities and Resources (75%), Manufacturing (73%), and Professional Services (67%). Financial Services shows 53%, Health Industries 37%, and Government and Public Sector the lowest at 16%. These premiums reflect acute talent shortages in AI implementation roles, particularly for hybrid skills combining technical proficiency (prompt engineering, system integration) with domain expertise. Figure 14 confirms these premiums correlate with productivity gains at AI-exposed companies, where wage growth for AI-skilled workers accelerated to 24.4% in 2025 versus 16.6% for least exposed firms. Crucially, Figure 16 shows AI specialist job postings are growing eight times faster than total postings, with Technology, Media and Telecoms accounting for 11.4% of sector roles by 2025. The report identifies three premium drivers: scarcity of talent capable of overseeing AI quality control (addressing [[ai's limitations]] in the ai-job-future-framework), demand for skills in atypical case management, and regulatory compliance needs. This underscores AI proficiency as a critical career accelerator, especially in 'superstar' companies achieving 163% productivity growth (Figure 12).

docs.title: Creative Skills
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-25

Creative skills represent the human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces. As Ferdman explains in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities involve innovation without relying merely on luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures.

docs.title: In Market Research Context
docs.text:
In the market research industry, creative skills are essential for:

  • Research design innovation: Developing novel methodologies to address emerging business questions
  • Insight generation: Making unexpected connections between data points to reveal deeper consumer truths
  • Problem reframing: Approaching research challenges from fresh perspectives
  • Visualization creativity: Presenting findings in compelling, memorable ways
  • Conceptual transformation: Adapting research frameworks to new market contexts

docs.title: Threats from AI
docs.text:
AI systems can create capacity-hostile-environments for creative skills when they:

  • Provide pre-packaged analytical templates that discourage novel research approaches
  • Generate standardized insights that reduce opportunities for creative interpretation
  • Automate routine aspects of research without preserving space for creative exploration
  • Replace the iterative process of creative development with instant AI-generated outputs
  • Undermine the habituation process necessary for developing creative expertise

docs.title: Maintaining Creative Skills
docs.text:
To preserve creative skills in an AI-augmented research environment:

  • Design research processes that intentionally create space for creative exploration before AI augmentation
  • Use AI as a brainstorming partner rather than a final decision-maker in insight development
  • Maintain opportunities for researchers to engage in the full habituation-process of creative skill development
  • Create environments that encourage risk-taking and learning from creative failures
  • Ensure researchers exercise agential-control over the creative direction of research projects

See habituation-process, agential-control, and plan-forming-vs-plan-following for related concepts.

docs.title: Epistemic Skills
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-25

Epistemic skills represent the human capacities related to knowledge acquisition, critical thinking, reasoning, and understanding. Drawing on Ferdman's structural analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these skills encompass both theoretical rationality (thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating) and practical rationality (phronesis or practical wisdom): doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason.

docs.title: In Market Research Context
docs.text:
In the market research industry, epistemic skills are fundamental to producing valuable insights that drive business decisions. These include:

  • Critical analysis: The ability to evaluate data quality, identify biases, and assess the validity of research findings
  • Interpretive reasoning: Making sense of complex data patterns and translating them into meaningful business implications
  • Evidence-based decision making: Using research findings to inform strategic choices rather than relying on intuition alone
  • Theoretical knowledge application: Appropriately applying research methodologies and frameworks to different business contexts
  • Skepticism and verification: Questioning assumptions and verifying findings through multiple data sources

docs.title: Threats from AI
docs.text:
As Ferdman argues, AI systems can create capacity-hostile-environments for epistemic skills when they:

  • Automate routine analytical tasks without providing opportunities for researchers to practice and develop their judgment
  • Present findings with high confidence that discourages critical evaluation (automation bias)
  • Replace the process of developing research questions with pre-packaged analytics
  • Reduce opportunities for researchers to engage in the habituation-process necessary for developing [[practical-wisdom]]

docs.title: Maintaining Epistemic Skills
docs.text:
To preserve and develop epistemic skills in an AI-augmented research environment:

  • Create capacity-conducive-environments that encourage researchers to exercise agential-control over the research process
  • Design AI tools that support rather than replace the development of practical wisdom
  • Ensure opportunities for embodied, intersubjective learning through mentorship and team collaboration
  • Maintain spaces for critical discussion and debate about research findings

See ai-deskilling-structural-problem, agential-control, and [[practical-wisdom]] for related concepts.

docs.title: Human intensive skills
docs.text: Human-intensive skills such as empathy, creativity, and face-to-face presence are increasingly important in AI-exposed roles.

docs.title: AI Deskilling and Core Human Capacities
docs.text: Recent research reveals that AI adoption poses specific risks to human-intensive skills through what Ferdman (2026) terms "capacity impoverishment." Unlike skill obsolescence in domains like hunting or basket-weaving, the deskilling of core human capacities diminishes us as humans and undermines our flourishing.

docs.title: Core Capacities at Risk
docs.text:
The following capacities are particularly vulnerable to AI-mediated deskilling:

  • Epistemic capacities: Theoretical rationality (thinking, considering reasons, forming beliefs) and practical rationality (phronesis or wisdom)
  • Social capacities: Moral capacity and abilities for developing meaningful relationships
  • Creative capacity: Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Volitional capacity: The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, and persevere

These capacities differ from technical skills because they are constitutive of human flourishing. As Ferdman explains, "the deskilling of our core human capacities is bad because inadequate development of these capacities can lead to 'capacity impoverishment,' which, in turn, diminishes us as humans."

docs.title: Structural Dimensions of Deskilling
docs.text:
Deskilling is not merely an individual responsibility issue. AI creates systemic conditions that inhibit capacity development through:

  • Capacity-hostile environments: That restrict action possibilities for capacity cultivation
  • Undermined habituation: Short-circuiting the gradual process of skill development
  • Reduced intersubjectivity: Diminishing opportunities for shared valuing of capacities
  • Disembodiment: Limiting physical presence necessary for certain capacities

For market research professionals, this means AI tools that automate data interpretation without preserving opportunities for researchers to develop critical thinking may ultimately undermine the quality of insights produced.

docs.title: Evidence of Deskilling
docs.text:
Studies show AI dependence leads to: - Erosion of critical thinking (Bonicalzi et al. 2023) - Decline in decision-making and analytical reasoning (Zhai et al. 2024) - Reduced activity awareness and competence maintenance (Rinta-Kahila et al. 2023)

See capacity-hostile-environments and ai-deskilling-structural-problem for related frameworks analyzing how AI affects human capacities.

docs.title: Senior skills
docs.text: Senior skills traditionally required in more senior positions that are now increasingly appearing in entry-level job descriptions due to AI adoption.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: New data from the PwC 2026 report quantifies the acceleration of 'seniorised' entry-level roles. Figure 8 reveals that in the US top AI exposure quartile, entry-level positions requiring traditionally senior skills (strategic decision-making, complex problem-solving, leadership) are projected to grow 35% between 2019-2025, while non-seniorised roles decline by 10%. This phenomenon occurs because AI tools automate foundational tasks previously performed by junior staff—such as data entry for [[inventory-clerks]] or CV screening for [[recruiters]] (Figure 2)—effectively compressing career ladders. Consequently, new graduates must now demonstrate competencies typically associated with 3-5 years of experience. Key senior skills appearing in entry-level descriptions include advanced data interpretation, cross-functional collaboration, and client relationship management, particularly in high-growth professionalised-jobs like environmental engineering. Figure 7 contextualizes this within broader market trends, showing high AI exposure quartile entry-level postings have flatlined since 2022, suggesting seniorisation may be a prerequisite for growth in AI-impacted roles. The report warns this trend could exacerbate early-career inequality without structured mentorship programs, while creating opportunities for accelerated career progression in organizations embracing the ai-job-future-framework.

docs.title: Social Skills
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-25

Social skills represent the human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life. According to Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these include moral capacity as well as social and caring capacities for developing meaningful relationships of friendship and love.

docs.title: In Market Research Context
docs.text:
In the market research industry, social skills are critical for:

  • Client relationship management: Building trust with clients through understanding their needs and constraints
  • Stakeholder communication: Translating complex research findings into actionable insights for diverse audiences
  • Team collaboration: Working effectively with cross-functional teams to design and execute research projects
  • Ethical research practices: Maintaining integrity in data collection and interpretation
  • Cultural sensitivity: Understanding diverse perspectives when conducting global research

docs.title: Threats from AI
docs.text:
AI systems can create capacity-hostile-environments for social skills when they:

  • Replace human-to-human interaction with AI-mediated communication
  • Reduce opportunities for embodied interaction necessary for developing moral agency
  • Create disembodied environments that make it harder to form meaningful professional relationships
  • Encourage researchers to become plan-followers rather than plan-formers in client engagements
  • Undermine the intersubjective dimension of skill development by removing human mentors

docs.title: Maintaining Social Skills
docs.text:
To preserve social skills in an AI-augmented research environment:

  • Prioritize face-to-face interactions for critical client discussions and complex problem-solving
  • Create structured opportunities for embodied, intersubjective learning through mentorship programs
  • Design AI tools that augment rather than replace human connection in research processes
  • Maintain spaces for shared valuing of social capacities through team reflection and discussion
  • Ensure researchers have opportunities to develop agential-control in client relationships

See embodiment-in-skilling, intersubjectivity-in-skilling, and capacity-conducive-environments for related concepts.

docs.title: Volitional Skills
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-25

Volitional skills represent the human capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow in order to achieve intrinsically valuable goals. As Ferdman explains in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this functions as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities, since developing and exercising any human capacity is difficult and requires willpower.

docs.title: In Market Research Context
docs.text:
In the market research industry, volitional skills are critical for:

  • Project management: Maintaining focus and momentum through complex, multi-stage research projects
  • Quality assurance: Persisting through detailed validation processes to ensure research integrity
  • Deadline management: Exerting effort to meet time-sensitive business needs
  • Overcoming research obstacles: Navigating unexpected challenges in data collection or analysis
  • Professional development: Committing to ongoing learning and skill enhancement

docs.title: Threats from AI
docs.text:
AI systems can create capacity-hostile-environments for volitional skills when they:

  • Automate challenging aspects of research that previously required perseverance and effort
  • Reduce opportunities to develop willpower through overcoming research difficulties
  • Create environments where researchers become plan-followers rather than plan-formers
  • Undermine the development of practical wisdom by removing opportunities to exercise judgment in unexpected scenarios
  • Replace the gradual habituation process with instant AI-generated solutions

docs.title: Maintaining Volitional Skills
docs.text:
To preserve volitional skills in an AI-augmented research environment:

  • Design research processes that maintain appropriate challenges requiring human effort and perseverance
  • Create capacity-conducive environments that encourage researchers to exercise agential-control over project direction
  • Ensure opportunities for researchers to encounter and overcome meaningful research obstacles
  • Maintain spaces for developing practical wisdom through handling unexpected research scenarios
  • Balance AI augmentation with opportunities for researchers to develop their volitional-capacity

See agential-control, habituation-process, and plan-forming-vs-plan-following for related concepts.

docs.title: Burning Glass Institute: Beyond the Binary
Overview
docs.text: Published in January 2026 by the [[burning-glass-institute]], "Beyond the Binary" represents a landmark analysis challenging the conventional wisdom that AI will either automate or augment jobs. Instead, the research demonstrates that automation and augmentation are frequently occurring simultaneously within the same occupations.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: The study analyzed labor-market data from millions of job postings across 759 occupations, developing metrics to measure both automation exposure (tasks AI can perform) and augmentation exposure (tasks where AI enhances human capabilities).

docs.title: Correlation of Automation and Augmentation
docs.text:
• Exposure to automation and augmentation is strongly positively correlated across occupations
  • Jobs most exposed to automation are also highly exposed to augmentation
  • This finding validates the "automation-augmentation paradox" first identified by Raisch & Krakowski (2021)

docs.title: Skill Demand Shifts
docs.text:
• Automation-exposed skills were 16% more likely to see demand decline compared to baseline skills
  • Augmentation-exposed skills were 7% more likely to see demand increase
  • This creates a net shift in the composition of work rather than simple job elimination

docs.title: The Entry-Level Challenge
docs.text: The report identifies a critical concern: junior workers traditionally built expertise through foundational tasks (drafting reports, conducting research, building models) that AI can now perform or accelerate. This threatens established apprenticeship models and expertise development pathways.

docs.title: Real-World Examples
docs.text:
• Project managers see routine scheduling automated while strategic coordination becomes more valuable
  • Analysts spend less time producing first-pass models but more time interpreting and communicating implications
  • Consultants can produce drafts instantly but face higher premium on the quality of underlying thinking

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: The study concludes that AI is not neatly dividing the labor market but is changing the composition of work inside jobs. Organizations risk "automating the developmental tasks before they have redesigned the learning pathway," potentially gaining short-term efficiency while weakening their future talent base.

docs.title: Update 2026-07-25
docs.text:
Expanded analysis of how AI systems undermine human capacities through structural conditions rather than individual failings. The paper introduces the critical distinction between capacity-hostile-environments and capacity-conducive-environments, analyzing how AI mediation can create environments with narrow fields of affordances that restrict opportunities for capacity development.

Key findings: - Deskilling is not merely an individual responsibility issue but a structural problem requiring societal solutions - Capacity cultivation (skilling) includes acquiring agential-control over capacities through a gradual process of habituation-process - Habituation depends on learning from others: both the "know how" of the skill and a shared understanding of the value of the skill - AI mediation risks undermining the quality of conditions for capacity habituation, leading to capacity impoverishment - artificial-personal-assistants may create capacity-hostile environments by encouraging plan-following rather than plan-forming

The paper argues for evaluating AI applications based on their conduciveness or hostility to capacity cultivation, and calls for societal obligation to foster capacity-conducive environments in the age of AI.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Market Research Institute International (MRII) 2026 global study represents the fourth annual comprehensive analysis of market research and insights professionals worldwide. Conducted by [[ed-keller]] and released at IIEX North America in May 2026, this research surveyed professionals across multiple regions to understand industry sentiment, AI adoption patterns, and evolving skill requirements in the insights sector.

docs.title: Professional Optimism vs. AI Readiness
docs.text:
• 58% of insights professionals believe their function will become more important in the future, demonstrating strong conviction in the field's relevance despite AI disruption
  • More than half report high levels of job satisfaction and expect the coming year to be better than the previous
  • This optimism exists alongside significant readiness challenges, creating what researchers describe as "the defining story of the insights industry today"

docs.title: AI Adoption Patterns
docs.text:
• Nearly 8 in 10 professionals report favorable views of generative AI
  • Approximately 50% use AI regularly in some capacity
  • Only 1 in 10 report AI is fully embedded in day-to-day workflows
  • Across 15 potential use cases (questionnaire design, data analysis, reporting), no single application has emerged as a dominant "killer app" (top adoption at ~40%)

docs.title: Skills Gap Analysis
docs.text:
The study identified a critical disconnect between: - Skills professionals want to develop: AI/digital skills, advanced analytics, technical capabilities - Skills leaders value most: business acumen, communication, ability to influence decisions, connecting insights to outcomes

This gap has significant consequences, as opportunities for learning and growth are among the biggest drivers of job satisfaction and retention.

docs.title: Value Chain Shift
docs.text:
As articulated by [[pam-forbus]] of Mondelez: "AI will increasingly answer questions, deliver insights, execute projects, and support stakeholders faster and at lower cost than ever before. That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

The study concludes that value is moving upstream - insights teams must evolve to shape decisions, drive growth, build AI-leveraging systems, and influence strategy rather than merely delivering answers.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: The study surveyed global market research professionals through structured questionnaires and follow-up interviews, with particular attention to AI exposure metrics and skill development priorities. It represents one of the most comprehensive longitudinal analyses of AI's impact on the insights industry.

docs.title: Pwc 2026 global ai jobs barometer
docs.text: PwC's comprehensive analysis of over one billion job advertisements examining AI's impact on the global labor market, powered by lightcast job posting data and orbis company financial data.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: This update incorporates detailed analysis of all 16 figures from the report. Key empirical findings include: A two-track jobs market has emerged where 52% of jobs are being democratized (AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans) and 22% are being professionalized (AI automates less expert tasks, leaving more expert tasks for humans) (Figure 2). Entry-level job postings in the highest AI exposure quartile have flatlined since 2022 (coinciding with ChatGPT's release), while lower exposure quartiles continue robust growth (Figure 7). Skills in AI-exposed roles are changing 2.2 times faster than in least exposed roles, with the gap widening annually (Figure 9). New tasks added to AI-exposed roles since 2022 are 2.5 times more likely to rely on human-intensive capabilities like empathy and creativity, quantified through the epoch-score (Figure 10). The report identifies a pronounced 'superstar effect' where the top 20% of AI-exposed companies achieve 5 times higher productivity growth (163% average) than the most exposed companies as a whole (33.5% in 2025) (Figure 12). Wage premiums for AI skills average 62% across sectors, ranging from 118% in Consumer Markets to 16% in Government (Figure 15). AI specialist job postings are growing eight times faster than total job postings, with Technology, Media and Telecoms leading at 11.4% of sector roles (Figure 16). These findings, derived from PwC's pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index, demonstrate AI's asymmetric impact on labor markets and validate the ai-job-future-framework's predictive power.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A comprehensive analysis of how AI adoption affects employment patterns across 21,559 U.S. firms, using observed AI spending data linked to workforce records. Published June 30, 2026 by Ara Kharazian (Ramp), Lisa Simon (Revelio Labs), and Ryan Stevens (Ramp).

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Linked Ramp's line-item spending data (identifying payments to AI vendors) with Revelio Labs' workforce records
  • Defined AI adoption as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  • Measured adoption intensity as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over first three months after adoption
  • Used Callaway-Sant'Anna framework for staggered treatment timing
  • Compared high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) vs. low-intensity adopters (bottom two PEPM terciles)

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
• High-intensity AI adopters grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Employment gains were broad across roles: engineering (+7.3%), sales (+10.3%), administration (+7.8%), customer service (+6.3%)
  • Gains emerged gradually, following what appears to be a "learning curve" as firms integrated AI tools
  • AI adoption is highly selected - adopters are larger, more technical, faster-growing firms
  • Early employment gains are concentrated in Information sector (13.4% growth for high-intensity adopters)
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment

docs.title: Methodological Innovations
docs.text:
• First study to combine observed firm-level AI spending with workforce records at scale
  • Introduced PEPM (AI spend per employee) metric to measure adoption intensity
  • Addressed selection bias by comparing early adopters to later adopters in the same intensity group
  • Provided evidence against the prediction that AI adoption will lead to broad job losses
